title: React fundamentals
blurb: Components, props, state, keys, rendering. The questions asked before anyone opens your portfolio. Code assumes React 19 with createRoot and StrictMode off, unless the question says otherwise.

questions.q: What is the `key` prop for?
choices: It is required by the linter but has no effect once the app is running
It sets the element's DOM `id`, so CSS and tests can select each item
It identifies a list item across renders so React can match it to its state
It sets the order in which sibling components are rendered and then mounted
questions.why: Without stable keys React matches list items by position. Delete the first row and every later row's state shifts up one: inputs keep the wrong values, checkboxes tick the wrong items. Keys never reach the DOM.
questions.asked: Universal. The strong answer describes the bug bad keys cause, not just the rule.

questions.q: When is using the array index as a key acceptable?
choices: When the list is never reordered, filtered, or added to except at the end
Always, because an index is a stable number that never repeats in a list
Never: React throws a warning and refuses to render index-keyed lists
Whenever the list is short, since reconciliation cost is what keys fix
questions.why: The index is only stable if positions are stable. A static list rendered once is fine; anything sortable, filterable or deletable needs a real id. Keys are about matching state to items, not about speed on long lists.
questions.asked: It tests whether you know the rule's reason well enough to know when it can be broken.

questions.q: What renders when `items` is an empty array?
choices: Nothing inside the div
An empty List component
An error: `0` is not a node
A literal 0 on the page
questions.why: `0 && ...` evaluates to `0`, and React renders numbers; it skips only booleans, `null` and `undefined`. Use `items.length > 0 && ...` or a ternary.
questions.asked: A tiny bug that ships to production constantly, so it is a quick filter question.

questions.q: What does this log on a single click, and what does `count` become?
choices: 0, and count becomes 2
0, and count becomes 1
1, and count becomes 2
2, and count becomes 2
questions.why: `count` is a constant captured by this render, so both calls set it to 0 + 1. The log shows the old value because setting state does not change the current render's variables. `setCount(c => c + 1)` twice would give 2.
questions.asked: The single best question for finding out whether someone understands React's render model.

questions.q: Why can this fail to update the screen?
choices: `push` throws in StrictMode, because state arrays are frozen in development builds
React compares references, so the same array looks unchanged and it may skip the render
The mutation corrupts the virtual DOM, so React has to discard the component tree
It updates fine; not mutating state is a style convention from the Redux era
questions.why: React bails out when `Object.is(prev, next)` is true, and a mutated array is still the same reference. `setTodos([...todos, newTodo])` gives React something new to compare. React does not freeze state, so nothing throws.
questions.asked: Constant. It links directly to the JavaScript reference-equality question.

questions.q: What is the difference between props and state?
choices: State holds objects and arrays; props hold primitives such as strings and numbers
Props trigger a re-render when they change; state changes never re-render
State is shared across the whole app; props are local to a single component
Props are passed in and read-only; state is owned and updated by the component
questions.why: If a value comes from above and the component never changes it, it is a prop. If the component owns it over time, it is state. If it can be computed from either, it should be neither: derive it during render.
questions.asked: The opener for most React screens; the derive-it-instead point is what lifts the answer.

questions.q: What is wrong with this?
choices: `count` is derived state; compute `items.length` during render
The dependency array should be `[items.length]`, not `[items]`
`setCount` cannot be called inside an effect without a guard
The effect needs a cleanup function that resets `count` to 0
questions.why: Storing derived state adds an extra render, a moment where the two disagree, and a synchronisation bug waiting to happen. Narrowing the dependency still keeps the redundant state. Anything computable from existing state or props should be computed.
questions.asked: One of the 'you might not need an effect' patterns from the React docs, asked often.

questions.q: What does 'lifting state up' mean?
choices: Moving component state into a global store so that any component can read it
Moving state into a context provider at the root of the application
Moving shared state to the closest common ancestor of the components using it
Moving state from a child into props, so that the child becomes a pure function
questions.why: Two siblings that must agree cannot each own the value, so the nearest ancestor owns it and passes down the value plus a setter. A global store or root context is a bigger move than needed; colocation says keep state as low as it can go.
questions.asked: It checks you reach for the smallest fix before a store or context.

questions.q: What is a controlled input?
choices: An input whose `required` and `pattern` rules are enforced by React
An input inside a `<form>`, so React manages its submission for you
An input rendered with `readOnly`, so users cannot change its value
An input whose value comes from state, updated through `onChange`
questions.why: Controlled means React state is the single source of truth, so you can format, validate or reset as the user types. Uncontrolled leaves the value in the DOM and you read it at submit: lighter, and fine for simple forms.
questions.asked: It usually leads into 'when would you choose uncontrolled?', which shows real form experience.

questions.q: What happens if you pass `value` without `onChange` to a text input?
choices: It works normally, and React reads the new value back on submit
The component throws on the first keystroke the user makes
The field cannot be edited, and React logs a warning about it
React silently switches it to an uncontrolled input instead
questions.why: React re-renders with the same `value` after every keystroke, so nothing typed appears, and it warns in development. Use `defaultValue` for an uncontrolled field, or add the `onChange` handler.
questions.asked: Everyone has hit the 'I can't type in my input' bug; this checks you know why.

questions.q: What is the virtual DOM, and why does React use one?
choices: A faster reimplementation of the browser DOM, used instead of the real one
A description of the UI that React diffs to work out the real DOM changes
A copy of the page kept in a Web Worker so rendering is off the main thread
A browser API that React polyfills in browsers which do not support it
questions.why: The value is not raw speed: hand-written DOM code is faster. The value is that you write `render(state)` declaratively and React works out the imperative steps. It lives on the main thread in ordinary JavaScript objects.
questions.asked: The wrong answer is 'because it's faster than the DOM'.

questions.q: When does a component re-render?
choices: When its state changes, its parent renders, or its context changes
Only when one of its props changes value, compared deeply
On every animation frame while the component is mounted
Only when the component calls `forceUpdate` or `setState`
questions.why: A parent rendering re-renders its children by default, whether or not their props changed; that is what `React.memo` opts out of. Re-rendering does not mean a DOM update; the diff may produce nothing.
questions.asked: The 'parent renders, child renders' default is the root of most React performance questions.

questions.q: Why does the input lose what you typed whenever `Parent` re-renders?
choices: `Child` needs a `key`, or React cannot match it between renders
An `<input>` cannot keep state unless it is a controlled input
`Child` is a new function each render, so React remounts it
`Child` is not wrapped in `memo`, so its state resets on render
questions.why: A new function on each render is a new component type, so React unmounts the old tree and mounts a fresh one: state gone, input cleared, effects re-run. A key or `memo` does not help because the type itself changes. Define components at module level.
questions.asked: A bug people hit when they extract a component 'for tidiness' inside another.

questions.q: How do you reset a child's internal state when a prop, such as `userId`, changes?
choices: Render the child with `key={userId}`
Call `setState` in an effect that depends on `userId`
Call `forceUpdate` on the child when `userId` changes
Wrap the child in `memo` with `userId` as a dependency
questions.why: A new key makes React treat it as a different instance, so it unmounts and remounts with fresh state. The effect works but renders once with stale state first. This is the documented alternative.
questions.asked: A neat trick that shows you have read the docs rather than only Stack Overflow.

questions.q: What is JSX, mechanically?
choices: A template language that React parses and interprets at runtime
HTML embedded in JavaScript and inserted as a string of markup
A browser-native syntax that React enables with a polyfill
Syntax compiled to function calls that create plain element objects
questions.why: `<Foo bar={1} />` compiles to a call producing `{ type: Foo, props: { bar: 1 } }`. That is why components must be capitalised: lowercase compiles to the string `'foo'`, not a reference. Nothing is parsed at runtime.
questions.asked: Knowing JSX is just function calls explains keys, capitalisation and why `if` cannot sit inside it.

questions.q: Why must hooks be called unconditionally at the top level?
choices: It is a lint convention only; React itself works with conditional hooks
React tracks hooks by call order, so a skipped call shifts later hooks
Conditional hooks run slower, because React cannot cache their results
Function hoisting moves hooks to the top, so conditions are ignored
questions.why: No name is attached to a hook, only its position in the call sequence. Skip one on a later render and the second `useState` reads the state belonging to the first. It is a correctness rule, not a performance one.
questions.asked: The good answer explains the mechanism rather than reciting 'the rules of hooks'.

questions.q: When should you use `useReducer` instead of `useState`?
choices: Whenever a component holds more than one piece of state at a time
When several values change together or transitions have real logic
Only when the app already uses Redux, so actions stay consistent
Whenever the state is an object rather than a primitive value
questions.why: A reducer moves the transition logic out of handlers into one pure function you can test on its own. For a wizard or a form with interdependent fields it is far clearer than five setters; for two unrelated values it is ceremony.
questions.asked: It tests judgement: a reducer everywhere is as much a smell as none at all.

questions.q: What does `user.age` show after the second click?
choices: 2, because the spread copies stale state
1, because objects never re-render
2, because updates to objects batch
3, because each click sees fresh state
questions.why: Each render closes over that render's state, and the second click happens after the re-render, so `user` is current. The stale-closure problem appears only when a handler is captured once: in an effect, a timer or a memoised callback.
questions.asked: It separates real stale-closure bugs from the imagined ones people add `prev =>` everywhere to avoid.

questions.q: What is 'colocating state'?
choices: Keeping state in the lowest component that needs it
Keeping all application state in one file so it is easy to find
Keeping state next to the CSS module whose styles it affects
Keeping shared state in context instead of passing it as props
questions.why: State lifted higher than necessary re-renders the whole subtree on every keystroke. Pushing it down is often a bigger performance win than any amount of `memo`, and it costs nothing.
questions.asked: The correct first answer to 'how would you fix a slow React page?'.

questions.q: An element keeps the same type and key at the same position between renders. What does React do?
choices: Unmounts it and mounts a fresh instance with the new props
Replaces its DOM node but carries the component state across to it
Keeps the DOM node and state, updating only the changed props
Warns about a duplicate key and renders both of the elements
questions.why: Reconciliation preserves the instance when type and key match at the same position. Change the type or the key and React tears down and rebuilds, losing state and re-running effects.
questions.asked: It is the rule underneath keys, remount bugs and the key-reset trick.

questions.q: Why does React batch several `setState` calls from one event into one render?
choices: So the calls run in the order they were made, which it could not otherwise do
So each render uses less memory, since fewer fibers are allocated at once
So server requests fired from the handler cannot race with each other
So the UI never shows a half-applied update and renders only once
questions.why: Three setters in one handler produce one render, so the screen never shows an intermediate state where one value changed and its partner did not, and no work is wasted. Since React 18 this also covers promises, timeouts and native handlers ('automatic batching').
questions.asked: The follow-up is usually 'what changed in React 18?', which is automatic batching.

questions.q: Which update to one list item is correct without mutating any existing state?
choices: `items[index].done = true; setItems([...items])`
`setItems(items.splice(index, 1, updated))`
`setItems(items.map(i => i.id === id ? { ...i, done: true } : i))`
`items.find(i => i.id === id).done = true; setItems([...items])`
questions.why: `map` gives a new array and a new object for the changed row, leaving the rest referentially identical, so memoised rows do not re-render. The spread options make a new array but still mutate the shared item object; `splice` mutates and returns the removed items.
questions.asked: A practical check: it needs both immutability and referential-equality reasoning.

questions.q: What is a fragment (`<>...</>`) for?
choices: Rendering its children only when a condition is true
Returning several elements without an extra DOM wrapper
Lazy-loading a subtree the first time that it is rendered
Grouping props so they can be spread onto children
questions.why: It avoids the 'div soup' that breaks CSS grid and flex layouts and table markup. Use `<Fragment key={id}>` when you need a key on it, since the short syntax cannot take props.
questions.asked: A warm-up; the key-on-a-fragment detail shows you have used it inside lists.

questions.q: What does `<StrictMode>` do in a production build?
choices: Nothing: its extra renders and effect re-runs are development-only
It double-renders components, but no longer re-runs any effects
It re-runs every effect once, to catch cleanups missing in prod
It throws on deprecated APIs instead of just logging a warning
questions.why: StrictMode's double render and mount-unmount-mount effect cycle exist to surface impure renders and missing cleanups while you develop; production builds skip them. So 'my fetch runs twice' in development is not a production bug, but the missing cleanup it reveals is.
questions.asked: It stops candidates 'fixing' StrictMode double effects with a ref guard that hides real bugs.

questions.q: How should a child tell its parent that something changed?
choices: By mutating the prop object, which the parent still holds
By dispatching a custom DOM event for the parent to hear
By calling a callback the parent passed down as a prop
By writing the value to a module-level shared variable
questions.why: Data flows down, events flow up. The parent owns the state and passes both the value and the updater, which keeps a single source of truth. Mutating a prop changes nothing React can see, so nothing re-renders.
questions.asked: The one-way data flow question every React screen includes in some form.

questions.q: What is wrong with this event handler?
choices: It calls `handleClick` during render and uses its return value
It must be `onclick`, because React mirrors the DOM attribute
It works, but creates a new handler function on every render
It fires twice per click, once for capture and once for bubble
questions.why: Pass the function (`onClick={handleClick}`) or wrap it (`onClick={() => handleClick(id)}`). As written it runs on every render, and if it sets state that is an infinite render loop.
questions.asked: A junior classic that shows whether JSX expressions are understood as JavaScript.

questions.q: `Counter` keeps a count in state. The user clicks it twice, then `isAdmin` flips. What is the count?
choices: 0, because a different JSX branch creates a new Counter
0, because changing the `label` prop resets its state
2, but only because both branches pass a string label
2, because the same type at the same position keeps state
questions.why: React reconciles by position and type, not by which line of JSX produced the element. Both branches put a `Counter` in the same slot, so React updates its props and keeps its state. Add `key="admin"` / `key="user"` to get separate instances.
questions.asked: It is the mirror image of the key-reset trick, and the bug it causes surprises even experienced developers.

questions.q: What is wrong with this checkbox?
choices: `onChange` fires on blur for checkboxes, so `done` updates late
It is uncontrolled, and `e.target.value` is the string `'false'`
`value` must be a string, so React throws on the boolean `false`
It works, but `e.target.value` lags one render behind the tick
questions.why: A checkbox is controlled with `checked` and read with `e.target.checked`; `value` is only the string submitted with the form. Here the box toggles on its own while `done` becomes the truthy string `'false'`. React's `onChange` fires on every click for checkboxes.
questions.asked: Copying the text-input pattern onto a checkbox is a common bug that reviewers catch.

questions.q: What does `n` show after one click?
questions.why: Updates queue in order: `setN(n + 5)` replaces the value with 5, then the updater receives the queued 5 and returns 6. An updater sees the pending value, while a plain value ignores what came before.
questions.asked: It checks whether you can reason about React's update queue rather than memorise 'use the updater form'.

questions.q: A component increments a module-level `renderCount` variable while rendering. Why is that unreliable?
choices: Module variables are reset each time the component re-renders
Module variables are read-only inside ES module components
React renders components inside a Web Worker, not the page
React may render a component more than once for one commit
questions.why: Rendering must be pure: React can render and discard work (concurrent rendering, StrictMode's double render in development), so side effects during render run an unpredictable number of times. Put side effects in handlers or effects.
questions.asked: Purity of render is the rule concurrent React depends on; interviewers probe it for senior-leaning mid roles.

questions.q: The user types into `Form`, then `showBanner` becomes true. What happens to the typed text?
choices: It is kept, because `false` held the first slot, so `Form` never moved
It is lost, because `Form` moves from the first to the second child
It is lost, because the parent `div` re-renders all of its children
It is kept, but only because `Form` stores its text in an uncontrolled input
questions.why: `{showBanner && <Banner />}` always occupies the first child slot; when false it renders nothing but still counts. So `Form` stays the second child with the same type and keeps its state. Re-rendering is not remounting.
questions.asked: It tests whether you understand how conditional JSX maps to positions in the tree.

questions.q: Why does `<myButton />` render an unknown HTML element instead of your `myButton` component?
choices: Components must be registered with React before JSX can use them
JSX tag names must match the file name the component is exported from
Lowercase JSX tags compile to strings, so they mean HTML elements
Components declared with `function` must be wrapped in `memo` first
questions.why: JSX treats a lowercase tag as the string `'myButton'` (an HTML tag) and a capitalised one as a variable reference. Rename it `MyButton`. There is no registration step in React.
questions.asked: A junior stumbling block that reveals whether JSX compilation is understood.

questions.q: What should a component return to render nothing?
choices: `undefined`, which React forbids and reports as an error
An empty string, which is the only safe empty value
`false` from a class component only, never a function
`null`, which React treats as an empty render
questions.why: Returning `null` is the idiomatic empty render. React 18+ also accepts `undefined`, and `false` renders nothing too, but `null` states the intent. The component still mounts, so its hooks and effects still run.
questions.asked: A quick one; the follow-up about hooks still running separates good answers.

questions.q: In `items.map(item => <Row item={item} />)`, where does the `key` belong?
choices: On the `<li>` that `Row` renders internally, as the list item
On the `<ul>` that wraps the list, so React can track the list
On `<Row>` inside the `map`, the element the array actually holds
On both `<Row>` and its `<li>`, so that each level can be matched
questions.why: Keys identify siblings in the array React receives, and that array holds `<Row>` elements. A key inside `Row` is on a single child, so it does nothing for the list, and React still warns.
questions.asked: It catches people who know keys are needed but not where, a warning seen in most junior code.

questions.q: In React 19 with `createRoot`, how many renders does the timeout callback cause?
choices: One, because React 18+ batches updates from timeouts and promises as well
Two, because batching applies only to updates made inside React event handlers
None until the next user event, because updates outside handlers are queued
Two, because each `useState` setter schedules its own render of the component
questions.why: Automatic batching (React 18+, needs `createRoot`) groups every state update made in the same tick into one render, wherever it came from: timeouts, promises, native listeners. Before React 18 only updates inside React event handlers were batched, which is where the 'two renders' belief comes from. `flushSync` is the opt-out when you need a synchronous render in between.
questions.asked: It checks that 'what changed in React 18' means something concrete to you rather than a release note.
